section.heading: Keep every agent moving, wherever you are.

items.title: Walk away. We’ll tell you when the agent needs you.
items.description: Threadbase watches the session and pushes you the moment the agent stops for input. Not a stream you have to babysit.

items.title: Approve without a tiny terminal.
items.description: Permission prompts and questions arrive as cards. Tap the answer. The agent keeps going.

items.title: Keep it fed.
items.description: Queue the next three prompts while the agent works. Dictate them. Attach a screenshot. It picks them up in order.

items.title: Start from your phone. Or take over.
items.description: Browse a machine's projects and launch a new session from the app — or adopt a session you started in your terminal and drive it from the phone.

items.title: Search everything.
items.description: Full-text search across every session on every machine, with snippets. Find the conversation where the agent explained that migration.

items.title: Every machine, one app.
items.description: Pair as many machines as you run. Each phone gets its own credentials you can revoke from the streamer at any time.

phoneStrip.heading: Built for the phone, not shrunk to it
items: A terminal view that strips the TUI decorations so the transcript reads like a transcript.
A chat view with diffs and tool calls, not a wall of ANSI.
Face ID lock, Markdown export, favourites.
English, Hebrew, Arabic, and Russian — with proper RTL.

security.heading: Your streamer. Threadbase can't read your sessions.
security.description: Threadbase runs on a streamer you install, and by default your phone talks straight to it — no Threadbase server in between. Sessions are end-to-end encrypted by default — Noise IK, X25519 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 — between your phone and each streamer. Every phone gets its own scoped credentials. Revoke one, and it's gone. Verify a machine's fingerprint with tb-streamer identity before you trust it.
cantSee: Your prompts, transcripts, approvals, and files are never readable by Threadbase. They don't touch a Threadbase server unless you turn on the optional relay, and even then they pass through it only as encrypted bytes.
Anonymous diagnostics — crash reports and basic stability data — are off by default and only ever sent because you switched them on.
Feedback you write in Settings goes out when you tap send, and nothing else does.
Keys live in the Keychain and Keystore.
security.scopeNote: This boundary describes the coding-session path. Pairing, notification delivery, and the local coding-agent process are separate parts of the architecture. The optional Threadbase Relay is a side service for people who want the simplest setup, with no tunnel, port forwarding, or VPN; it is off by default. If you turn it on, it can see that a connection happened — your IP address, timing, and sizes — but not what is inside it. The privacy policy has the details.

items.title: Provider details differ
items.description: Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot are all supported, but approvals, recovery, and resume behavior can differ by provider.

items.title: You run the streamer
items.description: Install the local streamer on every machine you want to reach and keep it accessible from your phone. Reaching it from outside your network is on you — a Cloudflare quick-tunnel helper is included, a guided setup isn’t yet.

items.title: Distribution is still beta
items.description: iOS ships through TestFlight; Android ships through closed testing on Google Play.

items.title: Platform edges
items.description: On Windows, sessions started outside Threadbase can’t report their working directory. Homebrew on Linux is x86_64 only — use npm on arm64. iOS Live Activities are opt-in on the streamer and need your own APNs credentials.

items.title: Some prompts still need the terminal
items.description: Single-choice approvals and questions work from the phone. Multi-select and multi-question forms fall back to the raw terminal for now.

socialProof.line: Open source, MIT, built by a developer who runs it every day.

items.question: Does it work with Codex?
items.answer: Yes. Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot sessions run side by side, with per-provider health and capability differences shown in the app.

items.question: Do I have to open ports?
items.answer: No. Pairing over your LAN works out of the box. A bundled Cloudflare quick-tunnel helper gets you off-LAN without touching your router.

items.question: What if my phone is offline when the agent asks?
items.answer: The push waits, and the session waits. Nothing times out because your phone was offline — open the app and you'll see what happened.

items.question: Which platforms run the streamer?
items.answer: macOS, Linux, and Windows. See the honest list above for the platform-specific edges.

items.question: Why is Sentry in the app?
items.answer: Two things you control: the feedback form in Settings, and Anonymous diagnostics — crash reports and basic stability data tagged with a random installation ID, off by default. Nothing is sent until you turn it on or tap send.

items.question: What does it cost?
items.answer: Threadbase is free and open source under the MIT license. Self-host the streamer on your own machines.

betas.headline: Join the Beta
betas.intro: Threadbase is available in early access on both iOS and Android. Pick your platform and get the mobile companion for Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot on your device.

platforms.name: iOS Beta
platforms.description: The iOS beta is open and ready to install through Apple's TestFlight program. No waiting, no approval — just tap the link on your iPhone or iPad.

steps.title: Install TestFlight
steps.body: If you don't have it already, download TestFlight from the App Store — it's Apple's official beta distribution app.

steps.title: Tap the invite link
steps.body: Open the "Join TestFlight" link above on your iPhone or iPad. TestFlight will open and show the Threadbase beta.

steps.title: Install and launch
steps.body: Tap "Install" in TestFlight. Once installed, open Threadbase and scan the QR code shown by the streamer on your workstation.

platforms.name: Android Beta
platforms.description: The Android beta runs through Google Play's closed-testing program. You'll need to join the testers group first, then opt in via Play — takes about 10 minutes end to end.

steps.title: Join the testers group
steps.body: Open the Google Group linked on the Android beta page and join with the Google account you use on your Android device.

steps.title: Wait ~10 minutes
steps.body: Google's tester-eligibility cache takes a few minutes to update after you join. Grab a coffee.

steps.title: Opt in on Google Play
steps.body: On your Android device, follow the opt-in link on the beta page, tap "Become a tester", then install from the Play Store.

androidBeta.headline: Join the Threadbase Android beta
androidBeta.intro: Google Play's personal-developer policy requires 12 testers over 14 days of closed testing before an app can go live. Help us hit that bar — installation is two clicks and a short wait.

steps.title: Join the testers group
steps.body: Click the button below to open the public Google Group. Sign in to the Google account you want to install on, then click “Join group” (no approval needed).

steps.title: Wait ≈10 minutes
steps.body: Google's tester-eligibility cache needs a few minutes to refresh after you join the group. Grab a coffee.

steps.title: Open the Play Store opt-in link
steps.body: On your Android phone, signed in to the same Google account, tap the second button. Then “Become a tester” → “Download it on Google Play”.

steps.title: Install and (optionally) pair
steps.body: Threadbase will install like any normal Play Store app, marked “(unreviewed)” while we're in closed testing. To use it, run tb-streamer on your workstation and scan its QR code.

fallback.title: If you see “App not available”
fallback.body: Wait another 15 minutes and retry — Play's permission cache occasionally lags. If it persists after 30 minutes, double-check you joined the group with the same Google account you're using on the phone.

androidBeta.closing: Once you're installed, you don't need to do anything else — your install counts toward the 12-tester gate just by staying on your phone.

privacy.heading: Privacy Policy
privacy.description: Threadbase is a thin client for the Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot sessions you run on your own computer, reached through a Threadbase streamer instance that you operate. Threadbase is local-first by design: your prompts, session content, and credentials stay on your device and on the streamers you configure.
privacy.intro: This policy describes the specific, limited cases in which data leaves your device, and the controls you have over each.
privacy.trafficHeading: The kinds of network traffic Threadbase uses
privacy.trafficIntro: Threadbase separates its traffic into eight distinct categories. Each is described in its own section below.
trafficCategories: Core traffic to your streamers — the app's normal function.
Push-notification delivery — optional notifications, including iOS Live Activities.
Crash reporting (Sentry) — automatic reporting is off by default and opt-in; a single crash can also be reported manually at any time.
User-initiated feedback submissions — only when you send feedback.
Optional screenshots or diagnostics you explicitly select — only when you choose to include them.
Newsletter subscription (MailerLite) — only when you opt in on the website.
Optional Threadbase Relay — only if you turn it on; it carries end-to-end encrypted traffic and sees connection metadata.
The Threadbase web app — only if you open it in a browser; its files are served by Vercel, which sees your IP address and request details.
privacy.coreBody: Threadbase connects only to the streamers you pair it with. By default it reaches them at the addresses you configure. If you have turned on the optional Threadbase Relay for a streamer (section 7), the app can also reach that streamer through the relay address the streamer provides. Session content, prompts, provider metadata, file attachments you send, and status events go solely to those streamers. By default, Threadbase does not route this traffic through any Threadbase-operated server. If you turn on the relay, the traffic passes through it only as end-to-end encrypted data the relay cannot read, and Threadbase does not copy it anywhere else. Your API keys and server credentials are stored on your device (in the iOS Keychain / Android Keystore) and are used only to authenticate to your own streamers.
privacy.pushBody: If you enable notifications, Threadbase registers a push token with each streamer you have paired, so that streamer can notify you when a session needs attention. The token itself is an opaque delivery address and does not contain your session content. Removing a server in Settings deletes its credentials from your device, and asks that streamer to delete its push token — though not if the streamer is unreachable at that moment; to be certain, go to Paired devices in Settings and revoke the device — that deletes the token immediately. Threadbase uses two delivery paths. Ordinary notifications — for example, a session waiting for your input — are delivered through Expo's push relay. That payload carries the project name, which may identify the repository or project, a fixed message, and the session and server identifiers the app needs to open the right screen — the server identifier defaults to that streamer's hostname unless a custom instance ID is configured; it does not include prompts, terminal output, credentials, or conversation content. Live Activities — the iOS lock-screen and Dynamic Island session status — are sent directly to Apple's push service (api.push.apple.com) by a streamer configured with Apple push credentials, which Apple issues per developer team. The Live Activity payload carries the session status, the project name, a title derived from your first message in that session, the session's start time, a server label that also defaults to the streamer's hostname, and a short, truncated excerpt of recent terminal output. The prompt-derived title and terminal excerpt can contain content from the session, including sensitive text that appeared there.
privacy.crashIntro: Threadbase can send crash reports, stability data, and limited network-performance diagnostics to Sentry to help diagnose defects. Sending these reports is off by default. Information reaches Sentry through two paths:
automaticReporting: Anonymous diagnostics. Off by default and opt-in. Nothing is sent automatically unless you turn on "Anonymous diagnostics" — in Settings, on the last onboarding screen if you see the option there, or by checking "Automatically send future crash reports and diagnostics" when you report a crash. Once it is on, future crashes, errors, and basic stability information about app sessions are sent automatically until you turn it off again. With Anonymous diagnostics enabled, Sentry also receives the fixed template of supported API routes (for example, /api/conversations/:id) and the decoded response-body size in bytes to diagnose excessive downloads. Actual resource identifiers, server addresses, query parameters, headers, and request or response contents are excluded. These records contain no resource or installation identifiers, are processed by Sentry in the European Union, and are retained according to the Sentry project’s configured log-retention period. Existing users are asked to accept the updated diagnostics notice before this collection starts.

Manual, one-time report. If the app crashes, the recovery screen offers a "Report this crash" button. Tapping it sends that single crash report even if Anonymous diagnostics is off. This is a deliberate action you take, not something the app does on its own, and it does not turn on Anonymous diagnostics. After you send feedback, the app may suggest turning it on; declining dismisses that one suggestion, and the suggestion appears at most twice in any 30-day period.
privacy.crashSameData: Automatic and manual JavaScript crash reports use the same in-app sanitization path described below. Native iOS and Android crashes are captured by the platform crash handler and may contain different native diagnostic data; server-side Sentry scrubbing is configured for that path.

crashReportingDetails.label: Service provider.
crashReportingDetails.bodyAfterLink: , a third-party error-monitoring service, under Sentry's own terms and data-processing agreements.

crashReportingDetails.label: What is sent.
crashReportingDetails.body: Only sanitized technical information: the app version and build number, the platform (iOS or Android), the operating-system major/minor version, the JavaScript engine, the release channel or environment, the Expo runtime version, the EAS update identifier, a generic connection-mode category (local, remote, or unknown), and the type, message, and stack trace of the error. When Anonymous diagnostics is on, reports also include basic stability information about app sessions — whether a session ended normally or with an error — used to measure release health. Reports also include an anonymous, randomly generated installation identifier used only to group reports; it is not tied to your identity, your device's advertising identifier, or your streamer credentials.

crashReportingDetails.label: What is excluded.
crashReportingDetails.body: JavaScript crash reports do not intentionally include prompts, terminal output, source code, file contents, credentials, authentication tokens, server addresses, hostnames, IP addresses, repository names or paths, session names or content, or your device name. A sanitization step runs in the app on every JavaScript report it sends, and anything that cannot be confidently sanitized is dropped rather than sent. Native crashes captured by the underlying iOS or Android platform layer are transmitted by that platform's own crash handler and may contain native diagnostic data outside the JavaScript allowlist; server-side Sentry scrubbing rules are configured for that path, including the exclusion of IP addresses.

crashReportingDetails.label: A note on absolutes.
crashReportingDetails.body: We design crash reporting to exclude the categories above, and we apply sanitization before sending. We cannot, however, describe unexpected behavior in the underlying SDK or platform as an absolute impossibility, which is why Anonymous diagnostics is opt-in and off by default.

crashReportingDetails.label: Your control.
crashReportingDetails.body: You can enable or disable Anonymous diagnostics at any time in Settings. Disabling it stops future reporting immediately and deletes the anonymous installation identifier from your device.

crashReportingDetails.label: Previously submitted reports.
crashReportingDetails.body: Reports already sent before you disable Anonymous diagnostics remain in Sentry subject to the retention below; disabling does not retroactively delete them.

crashReportingDetails.label: Retention.
crashReportingDetails.body: Crash reports are retained according to the configured Sentry project retention (by default, 30 days) and then deleted.

crashReportingDetails.label: Deletion requests.
crashReportingDetails.body: To request deletion of reports associated with your anonymous installation identifier where feasible, contact privacy@threadbase.sh.

crashReportingDetails.label: Processing location.
crashReportingDetails.body: Crash reports are processed by Sentry in the European Union. If you use Threadbase from outside the EU, your crash report is transmitted to and stored in the EU.

privacy.feedbackIntro: The Help & Feedback screen lets you send a bug report, feature request, or general feedback. This is always a deliberate action you initiate; Threadbase never sends feedback on its own.

feedbackDetails.label: What is sent.
feedbackDetails.body: The description you type, an optional reply email address if you provide one, and only if you leave the "Include technical diagnostics" option enabled, the same category of sanitized technical metadata described for diagnostics below. Before you submit, the screen shows you exactly what will be included.

feedbackDetails.label: How it is sent.
feedbackDetails.body: Feedback is delivered through the first available of: a configured feedback endpoint, the Sentry User Feedback channel when the build has Sentry configured, your device's email app, or a copy-to-clipboard option you can paste into the Threadbase feedback page. Tapping Send is explicit consent for that one submission and may use Sentry even when automatic crash reporting is off; it does not enable automatic reporting. Feedback works whether or not crash reporting is enabled.

feedbackDetails.label: Optional email.
feedbackDetails.body: If you provide a reply email, it is stored with your feedback so we can respond. Leaving it blank keeps your submission anonymous.

feedbackDetails.label: Retention.
feedbackDetails.body: Feedback submitted through Sentry is retained for the same period as crash reports (by default, 30 days) and then deleted. Feedback you send by email is kept until your request is resolved.

feedbackDetails.label: What is excluded.
feedbackDetails.body: As with crash reports, feedback does not intentionally include prompts, terminal output, source code, credentials, server addresses, or session content.

privacy.screenshotHeading: 5. Optional screenshots and diagnostics you select

screenshotAndDiagnosticDetails.label: Screenshots.
screenshotAndDiagnosticDetails.body: Threadbase never captures your screen automatically. If you attach a screenshot to feedback, you select it explicitly from your photo library, you can preview and remove it, and it is submitted exactly as you selected it. Attached screenshots are re-encoded to strip embedded metadata (such as location) and are size-limited. Screenshots are used only to deliver the feedback you submit and are not retained beyond what is necessary for that submission and its handling.

screenshotAndDiagnosticDetails.label: Diagnostics.
screenshotAndDiagnosticDetails.body: You can copy or export a diagnostics report from the app. It contains only the sanitized technical metadata categories described above, never prompts, terminal output, credentials, server addresses, session content, or your device name. You control whether it is copied or submitted.

privacy.screenshotReview: Screenshots and manually entered feedback may contain content you choose to include. Please review anything you attach before submitting.
privacy.newsletterBody: The Threadbase website offers an opt-in email newsletter for product news and updates. This is separate from the mobile app and only applies if you subscribe on the website. If you do, the email address you provide (and your name, if you choose to give one) is sent to MailerLite, our email service provider, which processes it under its own terms and data-processing agreements to send you the newsletter and manage your subscription, including confirmation and unsubscribe. Subscribing requires an explicit, unchecked consent checkbox — there is no pre-ticked opt-in. Every newsletter email includes an unsubscribe link; unsubscribing stops future emails and removes you from the list.
privacy.relayIntro: The Threadbase Relay is an optional hosted service for people who want remote access without setting up a tunnel, port forwarding, or a VPN. It is off by default. Your streamer connects to it only if you turn it on, and the app uses a relay address only for a streamer you have paired. If you never turn it on, nothing in this section applies and your sessions do not pass through any Threadbase-operated server.

relayDetails.label: What it carries.
relayDetails.body: Traffic between your phone and a streamer is end-to-end encrypted before it reaches the relay, using the keys of the phone and the streamer. The relay forwards encrypted bytes. It cannot read your prompts, transcripts, approvals, files, or terminal output, and it holds no key that could. It refuses unencrypted credentials rather than carrying them.

relayDetails.label: What it can see.
relayDetails.body: Connection metadata, while the traffic passes through: your IP address, a route identifier derived from your streamer's public key, the request method and path (which can include session identifiers), and the timing and size of each message. Because an IP address can identify a person, we treat this metadata as personal data.

relayDetails.label: What it records.
relayDetails.body: The relay's application logs record only event names (for example a connection opening or closing), a connection identifier, a shortened route identifier, and close codes. The route identifier is the first characters of an identifier derived from your streamer's public key. The logs do not record IP addresses, request paths, query strings, headers, or message bodies, and the relay writes no log line for each request. The relay also keeps aggregate counters, such as the number of requests, bytes relayed, and refusals, with no IP address, route, or connection identifier attached. To limit abuse, the relay holds a salted one-way hash of a client's address in memory only, which does not survive a restart. It also passes that hash, over the encrypted tunnel, to the streamer that receives the request. The relay does not use this data for advertising, behavioural analytics, or profiling.

relayDetails.label: Why we process it.
relayDetails.body: We process this metadata to deliver the connection and to keep the relay secure and working, including preventing abuse. Where the GDPR or the UK GDPR applies, our legal basis is our legitimate interest in running a secure, working service (Article 6(1)(f)).

relayDetails.label: Where it runs.
relayDetails.body: The relay runs on Fly.io, in its Amsterdam region in the Netherlands. Fly.io acts as our hosting provider and, in running the infrastructure, may process IP addresses and connection logs. Its infrastructure may also keep short-lived technical records of its own, for example about requests it could not complete. Its edge proxy also exports sampled request traces, which carry request metadata such as the hostname and path but not message bodies, to an observability service provider of its own. Fly.io does not publish a retention period for them. It is listed under service providers below.

relayDetails.label: Retention.
relayDetails.body: The relay stores no session content and has no accounts. Application logs are kept for up to 7 days, and aggregate counters for up to about 15 days, by our hosting provider. They contain no IP address and no session content.

relayDetails.label: Your control.
relayDetails.body: The relay is off by default. You turn it on or off on your streamer, and with it off the app reaches your streamer at its own address, as before. Contact privacy@threadbase.sh to ask about, or request deletion of, any data connected to you.

relayDetails.label: Open source.
relayDetails.bodyBeforeLink: The relay's code is public at
relayDetails.bodyAfterLink: , so these statements can be checked against it.

privacy.webIntro: The web app at app.threadbase.sh is the Threadbase app running in a browser instead of on your phone. It is optional. Everything above applies to it unless this section says otherwise, and if you never open it, nothing in this section applies.

webDetails.label: Where it runs.
webDetails.body: The web app is a set of files served by Vercel, which hosts it for us. When you open it, Vercel receives your IP address and the details of your request, as any web host does, and may keep them in its own server logs. Vercel does not receive your session content.

webDetails.label: Your connection to your streamers.
webDetails.body: Your browser connects directly to the streamers you pair, as the phone app does. Session traffic does not pass through Vercel or through any Threadbase-operated server, unless you turn on the optional relay. A streamer accepts a web page only if its operator has allowed the web app's address, which is off by default.

webDetails.label: What is stored in your browser.
webDetails.body: The web app stores your streamer URLs, API keys, and pairing credentials in your browser's local storage on your device. Browser local storage is not a secure credential store: the operating system's secure credential storage does not protect it, and other software or people with access to your browser profile may be able to read it. Pairing methods that need a secure device key are not available in the web app.

webDetails.label: Your control.
webDetails.body: Remove a server in the app, or clear this site's data in your browser, to delete the credentials the web app holds.

staysOnDevice: Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and other agent conversation content.
Terminal output and session content, apart from the prompt-derived title and truncated terminal excerpt an iOS Live Activity carries, described in section 2.

Your streamer URLs, API keys, and pairing credentials (in the iOS Keychain / Android Keystore). In the web app they are kept in your browser's local storage instead, which is not a secure credential store (section 8).
Your session names, favorites, and app settings.
privacy.uninstallBody: Uninstalling the app removes the Threadbase data stored in the app's own container. Some credentials held by the operating system's secure credential storage — such as the iOS Keychain — can survive an uninstall and be restored if you reinstall; to delete a server's credentials, remove that server inside the app first. Crash reports or feedback you submitted before uninstalling are not stored on your device and are governed by the retention terms above.
privacy.notCollectBody: Threadbase does not use advertising, tracking, fingerprinting, or behavioral telemetry. It does not include a product-analytics SDK. It does not automatically capture your screen, console output, or network request contents. With Anonymous diagnostics enabled, only fixed API route templates and response byte counts are collected as described in section 3. The only data that leaves your device is the core streamer traffic you direct (which, if you turn on the optional relay, passes through it end-to-end encrypted, as described in section 7), the optional push-notification token, and only with your action or opt-in consent, the crash reports, feedback, screenshots, diagnostics, and newsletter subscription described above. Separately, when Live Activities are enabled, the streamer sends the prompt-derived title and terminal excerpt described in section 2 to Apple's push service; that data travels from your streamer, not from your device.
privacy.localLogsBody: Your streamer writes operational logs locally on the computer where you run it. These can include timestamps and technical measurements such as event-loop delay and the number of open file descriptors. These measurements do not include prompts, terminal output, file paths, or credentials. Threadbase does not automatically send these local logs to Threadbase or Sentry. The app’s Anonymous diagnostics setting controls reporting to Sentry, not local streamer logging. You control access to and deletion of these files. If you choose to share a local log file, review it first: other operational entries can contain sensitive details.
privacy.subProcessorsIntro: Threadbase relies on the following third parties. Each one processes only the data described in its section above, under its own terms and data-processing agreements.

subProcessors.label: Expo.
subProcessors.body: Delivers ordinary push notifications. Expo receives your push token and the notification payload described in section 2, which carries no session content.

subProcessors.label: Apple.
subProcessors.body: Delivers Live Activities through the Apple Push Notification service. Apple receives your device's Live Activity token and the payload described in section 2, which includes a prompt-derived title, a server label that may be the streamer's hostname, and a truncated excerpt of session output; these may contain sensitive content.

subProcessors.label: Sentry.
subProcessors.body: Processes optional crash reports, stability diagnostics, and fixed API route templates with response byte counts, as described in section 3.

subProcessors.label: MailerLite.
subProcessors.body: Processes newsletter subscriptions from the website, as described in section 6.

subProcessors.label: Fly.io.
subProcessors.body: Hosts the optional Threadbase Relay. Fly.io's infrastructure handles your connection only if you turn the relay on, and may then process IP addresses and connection logs, as described in section 7. It cannot read the content, which is end-to-end encrypted. Fly.io is a US company certified under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework, with the UK and Swiss extensions.

subProcessors.label: Vercel.
subProcessors.body: Hosts the web app's files, as described in section 8. Vercel receives the IP address and request details of anyone who opens the web app, and may keep them in its own logs. It does not receive session content.

permissions.why: Scanning a QR code to pair with a streamer, and attaching photos to your sessions.
Attaching photos from your library to your sessions, and attaching a screenshot to feedback.

Converting your speech to text. On iOS Threadbase requests on-device recognition, subject to the device's available speech model; on Android it uses the system speech service and may send audio to Google.

Optionally locking access to your conversations. Authentication happens entirely on-device through the operating system (iOS Face ID/Touch ID, Android BiometricPrompt); Threadbase only receives a pass/fail result and never accesses, stores, or transmits your biometric data.
Delivering session notifications and iOS Live Activities, if you enable them. Section 2 describes what those messages carry.

yourControl: Anonymous diagnostics is off by default; enable or disable it any time in Settings.
Feedback and exported diagnostics are sent when you initiate them; optional automatic diagnostics, including API route templates and response sizes, require your consent.

Removing a server deletes its credentials from your device, and asks that streamer to delete its push token — though not if the streamer is unreachable at that moment. To be certain, go to Paired devices in Settings and revoke the device — that deletes its push token immediately, right from the app.

Uninstalling the app removes the data stored in its own container; credentials held by the operating system's secure credential storage, such as the iOS Keychain, can survive it — remove a server in the app to delete its credentials.
The optional Threadbase Relay is off by default. You turn it on or off on your streamer, and with it off the app reaches your streamer at its own address.
Contact privacy@threadbase.sh with any privacy question or deletion request.
privacy.operatorBody: Threadbase is operated by Ronen Mars, an individual.

globalError.heading: Something went wrong
globalError.body: An unexpected error interrupted this route. You can retry the render or return to the homepage.
